newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FDIC votes one-time thrift assessment.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FDIC votes one-time thrift assessment.

text.p: Federal regulators on Tuesday approved a one-time $4.5 billion assessment on the U.S. thrift industry to recapitalize the fund that insures depositors at savings and loans institutions to government-mandated levels.

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp also proposed to cut the premiums savings and loans pay twice yearly to fund the Savings Association Insurance Fund (SAIF), once the fund reaches the required level.
The one-time special assessment equals 65.7 cents for every $100 in insured deposits that thrifts hold.
The FDIC did, however, grant specific discounts and exemptions for certain institutions, including those classified as financially weak.
The special assessment, which stems from banking legislation passed recently by Congress, is due November 27.
The assessment is intended to bring the fund back up to the level at which it is equal to $1.25 for every $100 in insured deposits held by thrifts.
As of June 30, the SAIF had $3.9 billion, or the equivalent of 55 cents for every $100 in deposits.

Among those institutions that will receive a 20 percent discount on the assessment are certain "Oakar" banks, those institutions that belong to the Bank Insurance Fund but hold deposits that are treated as insured by the SAIF.

The FDIC granted exemptions to institutions classified as weak, although those institutions next year will pay insurance premiums based on existing levels. Those premiums range from 23 cents to 31 cents for every $100 in deposits, depending on the health of the institution.
The FDIC said 16 institutions fall under the weak classification.
The new premium schedule proposed by the FDIC would cut premiums to a range of zero to 27 cents for every $100 in deposits, depending on the health of the institution.
That schedule would take effect after the SAIF has been fully replenished later this quarter.
The FDIC proposed a complicated premium schedule for the fourth quarter that will represent a transition to the new schedule.
